introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **e)** Parents should choose spouses for their children. Do you agree?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the tradition and my position (disagree, with nuance).
2. The arguments for parental choice (experience, family unity, stability).
3. Why they fail: marriage is personal; money cannot create love.
4. The changed world: education, the law, the consequences of force; selfish motives.
5. A compromise: guidance, not decision.
6. Conclusion.

**Model composition (537 words)**

Marriage is one of the most important decisions in a person's life, and in many African societies, parents have traditionally played a leading role in it. Some families still select a husband or a wife for their children, arguing that parents have more experience and wisdom. Whether this practice is good is a question that divides opinion. In my view, parents should advise and guide their children, but they should not choose their spouses for them.

Those who support the traditional system give some serious arguments. Firstly, parents know the character and history of the families concerned, and they may notice dangers that a young person in love fails to see, such as violence, dishonesty or serious illness in a family. Secondly, marriage in our culture unites two families, and the approval of the elders brings support, prayers and stability to the couple. Finally, supporters recall that many marriages arranged by parents in the past lasted for fifty years, and that divorce was rare. They conclude that young people, who are carried away by emotions, are poor judges of a life partner.

These arguments are not without value, but they are weakened by several facts. To begin with, a marriage is above all a relationship between two individuals who will share the same house, the same bed and the same troubles for decades. Only the two of them know whether they feel respect, attraction and trust. A parent may choose a rich or respected family, but money and status cannot create love. A girl or a boy who is forced to live with a stranger may endure years of silent misery, and the marriage may last only because divorce is shameful and not because it is happy.

Moreover, the world has changed. Today, young people meet at school and at work, so they can know their partners before marriage. Education has given them the ability to think for themselves, and modern law requires the free consent of both persons. Forcing a young person into marriage is therefore not only unfair but also unlawful. Forced unions often end in unhappy homes, quarrels and unfaithfulness.

Furthermore, parents are not always objective. Some choose a partner for selfish reasons, for example to obtain a bride price, to settle a debt or to protect the family's land. In such cases, the child becomes an object of trade, not a person with feelings and rights.

Nevertheless, I do not suggest that young people should ignore their parents completely. Parents have wide experience and often see more clearly. The best solution is a partnership: the young person chooses, the parents are consulted and may investigate the background of the partner, and both sides discuss any doubts calmly. If the parents raise a serious objection, the young person should listen carefully, because love can blind. But the final decision, being a matter of lifelong happiness, must belong to the two people who will live it.

In conclusion, I disagree that parents should choose spouses for their children. They should be advisers and not judges. A marriage entered freely, with the blessing of the family, has the best chance of producing a happy home, and a happy home is the foundation of a healthy society.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Answering only 'yes' or 'no' with one-sided arguments: a good answer to 'Do you agree?' meets the opposite view fairly before rejecting or limiting it.
